title: CHAPTER TWENTY-EIGHT. On the mode of production, parts, marriage, possession, and chief dignity of humankind
english: CHAPTER TWENTY-EIGHT. On the mode of production, parts, marriage, possession, and chief dignity of humankind.

Thus far concerning the origin of humankind as far as concerns his principle, namely God, whose being, existence, self-sufficiency, and power variously weighed: there follows the MODE by which humankind arose, which is his production from red earth with the breath of the spirit of life according to the image and likeness of the Creator.

Humankind, as he was the last of creatures, was also the compendium of all creatures both immediately and mediately perfect, participating their nature as to spirit and these as to body: the epitome of the world, the horizon of time and eternity. He was moreover also the end of those mediately perfect, and therefore viewed in them and above them with respect to the Creator's intention. Therefore he is said to have been created in another mode than the other creatures. For those were produced by the Word alone: Let there be light, let there be an expanse, and so on; but humankind as if by greater counsel and deliberation: Let us make humankind — Genesis 1:26 — whose image's reason is declared to us by (1) Christ's human nature, pure and whole as in Adam before the fall; (2) human nature glorified in heaven; (3) universal sin, which succeeded into the place of this lost image; (4) begun renovation, by which it begins to be restored in us — Colossians 3:10; Ephesians 4:24.

title: II–VII: definition; essential parts — body and rational immortal spirit
english: II. Humankind is the last of creatures, made by GOD through the Word from the dust of the earth, and by breath into his nostrils made a living soul, endowed with immortal rational spirit according to the image of God after His likeness. Briefly and in the philosophical manner humankind is defined a rational animal; we here, considering him in order to his creation, have described him from the biblical text — Genesis 1:26–27; 9:6; Ecclesiastes 7:29; Acts 17:28; 1 Corinthians 11:7.

III. In humankind there are to be considered essential parts, sex, and finally proper affections. IV. His essential parts are the animated body and the rational spirit. V. The human BODY is his visible part, a fleshy structure supported by bones and covered by skin, animated by breath — Genesis 2:7; Job 10:11; Matthew 6:25; 1 Corinthians 12:12. VI. The rational and immortal SPIRIT is the invisible part of humankind, powerful with intellect and will, so united to the human body that nevertheless it can be separated from it — Genesis 2:7; Zechariah 12:1; Matthew 10:28; Acts 7:59; 2 Corinthians 5; 12:2; 1 Thessalonians 5:23; Revelation 6:9. VII. This spirit, though it dwells in the body, is through itself an essence without body.

title: Mind above elements; intellect, will, executive power
english: We believe that to the well-formed body and living soul — which humankind has in common with all fishes and birds of the fifth day and terrestrial animals of the sixth, Genesis 1:20 and 30 — adorned, the mind sent in by God is coupled, which we confirm by these REASONS to be more divine than the vegetative and sensing soul. (1) Because no effect is elevated above its principal and adequate cause. Therefore the human soul is in reality more divine than the sensing spirit. The human mind, both by understanding and by seeking, thinks above the sun and the heaven of heavens and worlds however many, and always understands something beyond what it knows, into infinity. From which we conclude that it is not an effect of sun and elements, as the sensitive spirit is, but the offspring of the Infinite whom we call God.

VIII. The faculties of the rational soul are these. IX. Intellect is the faculty of the soul by which we apprehend, discern, and either approve or disapprove objects under the reason of truth — theoretical and practical; here observation and conscience. See Ames, Book 1 on conscience. X. Will is the faculty of the rational soul which seeks objects under the reason of good and turns from evil. The nature of this faculty is not to be compelled, and according to its first institution to be restricted by no necessity to extremes. XI. Executive power is the faculty of the soul by which we effect or impede or at least permit practical objects.

title: XII–XVI: sex; male and female; first parents Adam and Eve
english: XII. So much concerning the essential parts of humankind: there follows sex, by which, distinguished by the organs of generation, he furnishes origin to his descendants. XIII. And humankind according to sex is male and female. This difference of sex is necessary for generation, and so for the perfection of the human race. For each being is then called perfect in physics when it can generate its like. Therefore, since the male alone cannot generate, he is not altogether judged perfect for the consummation of his genus unless he also have the other portion of himself. On that account Christ in Matthew 19:4, praising Moses' text, says: Have you not read that the Maker from the beginning made male and female? And Moses in Genesis 2:18: It is not good that the human be alone; I will make him a help that is before him. And in verses 21–22 the Lord God caused Adam to sleep with deepest sleep, drew out one of the ribs, and constructed the woman from that rib.

XIV. Sex shines forth both in the first parents and in their descendants. XV. The first parents are the first humans. XVI. Adam was the first man, divinely formed; Eve the first woman, constructed from Adam's rib.

title: XIX: marriage; paradise prepared for the first pair
english: XIX. MARRIAGE is the covenant by which male and female are joined into one society of life for mutual help, the generation and education of offspring, and the conservation of chastity. Concerning the marriage of Adam and Eve see Zanchi on the works of God and others.

That garden of paradise was so prepared that it was most conveniently inhabited by the first parents: a pleasant place, distinguished by the trees of life and of the knowledge of good and evil, irrigated by rivers. Yet it is to be held that paradise did not lie open so widely as the whole world, nor is it to be sought everywhere by the allegorical deliriums of the Origenists. All those views are to be rejected which either invent paradise as merely allegorical or place it outside this earth against Moses' historical narration in Genesis 2:8–15.

title: Image and likeness of God in the whole human; natural and supernatural
english: There follows the affection of humankind, which is that the whole human, both by soul and by body, was created according to the image of God and after His likeness, in which his highest perfection is beheld. Image differs from likeness as species from genus; among some, likeness is the exegesis of image, as if it were said the most similar image of God — Genesis 1:27; 5:1.

The word image signifies either the archetype itself to whose exemplar another is made, or that which is made toward another. In the former acceptance only Christ can be called the image of God; in the latter, the image of God is beheld in no visible thing except in humankind. We assert that its subject first and through itself is the rational soul, most beautifully adorned with the gifts of justice, holiness, and truth. Yet we do not altogether exclude the human body from the reason of this image. Rightly, therefore, the whole human is said to have been created according to the image of God — which is clear even from the restoration of this image, in which not only the soul but the whole human, and even the body itself, is so restored as to be the temple of the Holy Spirit. And the image of God exists not in the man only but also in the woman, though in the man it is more illustrious.

title: Natural and supernatural parts of the image; Cap. 28 close toward governance
english: The parts of this image can be distinguished thus: some are natural to the human, some supernatural; some essential, some accidental; some belong to him wholly, others according to some part — namely soul or body. What is natural and essential to the soul is to be a spirit and endowed with the faculty of understanding and willing both according to nature and according to the mode of freedom. What is supernatural and accidental: the knowledge of God and of things required for eternal salvation, which comes under the name of wisdom, and the rectitude and holiness of the will according to that knowledge. Immortality is thus far essential to the soul that it cannot die unless it cease to be; but supernatural and accidental insofar as it is from grace and the assistance of conservation. To the body, immortality is wholly supernatural and accidental. To the whole human externally belongs dominion over creatures.

Moreover that image of God which humankind is said to have lost in the fall was not wholly natural but supernatural, granted by God's peculiar gift — justice, innocence, integrity: in the intellect, supernatural knowledge of God's essence and will; in the will, the highest inclination to known good, or the highest obedience and subjection toward God; in the appetite, the highest concord with reason. Finally the end for which humankind was thus created is that he would acknowledge, love, and worship his Creator God and live blessed with Him forever — by which act of creation God most clearly exhibited the glory of His wisdom, goodness, and power.
